#

(Benjamin) Gayelord Hauser
Gayelord Hauser was an American nutritionist and self-help author who became one of the twentieth century's first celebrity diet gurus, urging followers to eat natural, unprocessed foods and counting Greta Garbo among his Hollywood clients.
  • “Columns produced debonair style” · 1966
(Bishop) Charles Perry
Charles Perry was the first Anglican Bishop of Melbourne, arriving from England in 1848 to lead a diocese with barely a handful of clergy, and going on to help found Melbourne Grammar and Geelong Grammar schools.
  • “Wowser” · 1968
  • “The Theatre Evil and the Evil of Dancing” · 1968
(Bishop) James Moorhouse
James Moorhouse was the second Anglican Bishop of Melbourne, a member of the church's liberal 'broad' wing whose 1877 invitation to the visiting Shakespearean actor William Creswick to give dramatic readings at Bishopcourt scandalised more conservative clergy, as Keith Dunstan recounted in 'Wowsers'.
  • “The Theatre Evil and the Evil of Dancing” · 1968
(Dean) Hussey Burgh Macartney
Hussey Burgh Macartney was Dean of Melbourne from 1852 until his death in 1894, having sailed out from Ireland with Bishop Charles Perry in 1847 to help establish the fledgling Anglican Church in the colony.
  • “Wowser” · 1968
(Pastor) Sid Denton
Sid Denton ran the Jigalong Apostolic Mission in the Western Australian desert, caring for Aboriginal people newly come in from the bush, which Keith Dunstan visited and wrote about during his 1960s outback flying tour.
  • “Columns produced debonair style” · 1966
(Reverend) H. Worrall
The Reverend H. Worrall was a Geelong Methodist minister whose outrage at the murder of bookmaker 'Big Mick' McLeod at Flemington Racecourse turned him into the unlikely leader of Melbourne's 1906 anti-gambling crusade, culminating in a march on Parliament House with thousands of followers singing 'Onward Christian Soldiers', an episode Keith Dunstan told at length in 'Wowsers'.
  • “The Gambling Evil” · 1968
(Thich) Quang Do
Thich Quang Do was a Vietnamese Buddhist monk who became the public face of the Buddhist uprising against the Diem government in the early 1960s, and who was later gaoled and held under house arrest for decades as a leading dissident against Vietnam's Communist regime.
  • “Essentially worldly columns” · 1966
1956 Olympic Games
The 1956 Melbourne Olympics were the first Games held in the Southern Hemisphere, nicknamed the 'Friendly Games', and opened by Prince Philip after a tour of Papua and New Guinea that Keith Dunstan covered as a young reporter.
  • “Columns on HM and HRH” · 1966
  • “The Athletic Passion” · 1973
1960 Tokyo Olympics
Tokyo was preparing to host the Olympic Games (held in 1964) when Keith Dunstan visited Japan at Christmas 1963 and was shown around the half-built Games venues by an over-enthusiastic public relations official.
  • “Essentially worldly columns” · 1966
1962 Commonwealth Games
The 1962 British Empire and Commonwealth Games were held in Perth, where photographers still smarting from a Chelsea Flower Show soaking planted a sprinkler in Prince Philip's path and got the retaliatory royal outburst that finally gave Keith Dunstan's royal tour reporting a decent story.
  • “All I know about ethics, I learned at sword-point” · 17 Jul 2011
1963 Royal Visit to Australia
Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip toured Australia from February to March 1963, taking in every state and the outback for the first time, a trip Keith Dunstan covered as a Royal Tour reporter.
  • “Royal columns” · 1966
2/4th Field Regiment
The 2/4th Field Regiment was an Australian artillery unit raised in Melbourne in 1940 that served in the Middle East, Syria and New Guinea during the Second World War; Keith Dunstan's brother Bill was an original member.
  • “Following a VC” · 1990

6 Oclock swill
The six o'clock swill was the mad rush to down as many beers as possible before hotel bars shut at 6pm, a wartime austerity measure that lingered in Victoria until 1966 and which Keith Dunstan remembered as a defining, faintly absurd feature of 1950s Melbourne drinking.
  • “Columns produced debonair style” · 1966
  • “1966 and All That” · 01 Dec 1966
  • “The Evil of the Demon Drink” · 1968
  • “APITS” · 1990
  • “The Beer Demon” · 1994
7th Battalion
The 7th Battalion was an Australian infantry unit that fought at Gallipoli, including the desperate defence of the captured trenches at Lone Pine in August 1915, where four of its men, including Keith Dunstan's father William Dunstan, won the Victoria Cross.
  • “Following a VC” · 1990

A Place in the Sun
A Place in the Sun, or APITS, was the daily column Keith Dunstan wrote for Melbourne's Sun News-Pictorial for twenty-seven years from 1958, a column that had actually run since the paper's first edition in 1922.
  • “Supporting a column” · 1966
A. G. Grant
  • “Rembrandt and Phar Lap” · 05 May 1962
Abbotsleigh
Abbotsleigh is an exclusive girls' school founded in 1885 that has stood at Wahroonga on Sydney's North Shore since 1898; Keith Dunstan noted it as the strait-laced alma mater of the eccentric Sydney identity Bea Miles.
  • “Beatrice Miles” · 1980
Aborigines
Aboriginal Australians are the continent's First Peoples, with a continuous culture stretching back tens of thousands of years before European settlement in 1788; Keith Dunstan wrote about Aboriginal communities and individuals he encountered across his travels and profiles.
  • “Christmas across a continent” · 01 Dec 1963
  • “Xavier (Alfred Francis) Herbert” · 1980
Adam Lindsay Gordon
Adam Lindsay Gordon was a nineteenth-century poet, horseman and politician whose bush ballads about riding and the Australian landscape made him one of the country's first widely celebrated literary voices.
  • “Strictly personal columns” · 1966
  • “The Australian Landscape” · 1972
  • “The Australian Character” · 1972
Adelaide
Adelaide is South Australia's capital, a city Keith Dunstan alternately admired and teased in his Bulletin writing, whether comparing its cultural ambitions with Melbourne's or tracing Australia's earliest artificial ice-skating rinks.
  • “Goodbye to the Glaci” · 27 Apr 1963
  • “Alexander Tolmer” · 1980
Adelaide Festival of Arts
The Adelaide Festival of Arts is Australia's oldest major arts festival, launched in 1960, whose growing reputation Keith Dunstan cited more than once in the Bulletin as proof Melbourne's own Moomba festival needed to lift its game.
  • “The New Image” · 03 Mar 1962
  • “Rembrandt and Phar Lap” · 05 May 1962
  • “Battle of the Flower” · 01 May 1965
Adelaide News
The Adelaide News was the afternoon newspaper a 22-year-old Rupert Murdoch inherited in 1953, and which he turned into a scandal-filled tabloid that became the launching pad for his global media empire.
  • “Walking the tightrope” · 1990
Adelaide Oval
Adelaide Oval is South Australia's premier sporting ground, the sodden 'sacred altar of black mud' where Victoria fought back from a rare MCG interstate football loss in 1963, a revenge match Keith Dunstan covered as a genuine cause célèbre.
  • “Vengeance on a Black Mud Altar” · 20 Jul 1963
Adolf von Baeyer
Adolf von Baeyer was the German chemist who in 1878 synthesised indigo dye, a breakthrough that, as Keith Dunstan noted, ruined the natural indigo trade of India and China while guaranteeing denim makers a reliable supply of blue.
  • “The Humble Uniform” · 1995
Adrian Benns
Adrian Benns was a wartime friend of Keith Dunstan's who turned up unannounced on the island of Labuan during his RAAF service in 1945, and who years later joined him on the North Victorian wine trip that first drew Dunstan into wine.

  • “Finding the wine demon” · 1994

Adrian Rawlins
  • “Not Only Serious – Solemn!” · 02 Jun 1962
Air Training Corps
The Air Training Corps was a wartime youth organisation set up in 1941 to prepare teenage boys for RAAF service, giving cadets like Keith Dunstan priority in the call-up when they turned eighteen.

Albert Park
Albert Park is the bayside parkland just south of the Melbourne CBD, built around an artificial lake that became, in Keith Dunstan's telling, the site of a years-long losing battle against an invasive Canadian waterweed, and which developer Stanley Korman once proposed topping with his own Eiffel Tower.

Albert Sefrankel
Albert Sefrankel was, by the legend Keith Dunstan recounted, the Frankfurt trader who did a deal with an American serviceman for six pairs of army-surplus denim and went into jeans manufacturing himself in 1949.
  • “The Humble Uniform” · 1995
Albert Tucker
Albert Tucker was a largely self-taught Melbourne painter and a leading figure of the 1940s Angry Penguins modernist circle alongside Sidney Nolan and Arthur Boyd, known for expressionistic works shaped by wartime unease.

Albury
Albury is the New South Wales town on the Murray River where Melbourne's and Sydney's differently gauged rail lines first met in 1883, forcing generations of interstate travellers to change trains there, and which Keith Dunstan used as shorthand for the old Sydney-Melbourne rivalry, once floating it as the site for a summit between premiers Bolte and Heffron.

Albury-Wodonga
Albury-Wodonga is a twin-city region straddling the Murray River on the New South Wales-Victoria border, made a focus of national growth planning in the 1970s as a decentralised alternative to Sydney and Melbourne.

Alderman Hills
Alderman Hills was Lord Mayor of Sydney in the mid-1960s, who joined Keith Dunstan aboard the inaugural Canadian Pacific Airlines flight over the North Pole and exchanged greeting cables with Australians stationed at Mawson in Antarctica.

Alexander Colquhoun

Alfred Deakin

Ali Bacher
Ali Bacher captained South Africa and later administered its cricket, describing the cancelled 1971 Australian tour as the final nail in the coffin of a side already isolated by apartheid.

Alice Springs
Alice Springs is the main town of Central Australia, founded in the 1870s as an Overland Telegraph repeater station on Arrernte land and later named after Alice Todd, wife of the telegraph superintendent.

Alick Wickham
Alick Wickham was a Solomon Islands-born swimmer who came to Sydney for schooling in 1898, and whose spectacular over-arm stroke at the Bronte pool prompted a watching coach's cry of 'crawling'—one of two rival origin stories Forbes Carlile traced for the Australian crawl.

All Nippon Airlines (ANA)
All Nippon Airways is Japan's largest airline, formed in 1957 from a merger of two small domestic carriers; Keith Dunstan and a travelling companion once boarded the wrong ANA flight in Japan and nearly ended up in Hokkaido.

All Saints Winery
All Saints is a historic winery at Wahgunyah in Victoria's Rutherglen region, founded in 1864 by Scottish immigrants George Sutherland Smith and John Banks, whose castellated cellar building is now run by successive generations of the Sutherland Smith family.

Allan Wilkie

Anatole de Montaiglon
Anatole de Montaiglon (1824-1895) was a French librarian and art historian who specialised in medieval literature; his praise for the painting Chloe was cited by Keith Dunstan in retelling Melbourne's scandalised reaction to the nude when it went on display in 1883.

Andre Simon

Andrew 'Boy' Charlton

Andrew Fisher

Andrew Hickinbotham
Andrew Hickinbotham was a viticultural consultant from Australia's well-known Hickinbotham winemaking family who helped establish Keith Dunstan's own small pinot noir vineyard on the Mornington Peninsula in the late 1980s.

Andrew Peacock
Andrew Peacock was a long-serving Liberal politician and twice leader of the federal Opposition through the 1980s and early 1990s, whose reported habit of keeping a car-boot fax machine and cellular phone struck Keith Dunstan as the emblem of a newly gadget-obsessed Australia.

Anglicanism
Anglicanism is the Protestant tradition descended from the Church of England, established when Henry VIII broke from Rome in 1534; Keith Dunstan wrote about wrestling with faith and eventually being drawn to its High Church wing as a young journalist in Brisbane.

Annie Besant
Annie Besant was an English freethinker and birth control advocate whose pamphlet 'The Law of Population' triggered a landmark 1888 Sydney obscenity prosecution, resolved in her favour by a judgment Keith Dunstan quoted at length in 'Wowsers' as decades ahead of its time.

Annie Oakley
Annie Oakley was the celebrated sharpshooter of Buffalo Bill's Wild West show, invoked by Keith Dunstan as the model for the 1930s New York divorcee playing at horse riding on a Reno dude ranch while waiting out her residency.

Anthony Eden was British Prime Minister from 1955 to 1957, whose government's botched military intervention in the 1956 Suez Crisis, after Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal, forced his resignation on grounds of ill health.

Anthony Hanson is a British Master of Wine and Burgundy specialist whose 1982 book Burgundy became a standard reference; Keith Dunstan drew on his memorable description of pinot noir's aroma in writing about his own vineyard.

Anthony Trollope
Anthony Trollope was one of the most prolific English novelists of the Victorian era, best known for his Barsetshire series of novels chronicling the everyday life and social mores of middle-class England.

Anti-Football League
The Anti Football League was a tongue-in-cheek club Keith Dunstan founded in his newspaper column in 1967 for Melburnians weary of the city's football obsession, which went on to raise large sums for charity through stunts like anti-Grand-Final tickets and its annual Wilkie Medal.

Anzac Day
Anzac Day, held every 25 April, commemorates the 1915 Gallipoli landing and Australia's war dead; for Keith Dunstan's family it was a fraught annual ritual, the one day his Victoria Cross-winning father allowed himself to remember, and briefly relive, the horror of Lone Pine.

Ararat
Ararat is a western Victorian city and Henry Bolte's home electorate, briefly notorious in 1963 for the dawn killing of its beloved pet carp, Napoleon, by a Fisheries and Wildlife inspector, an act the Premier himself mourned to Keith Dunstan.

Archer
Archer was the Sydney horse that won the first two Melbourne Cups, in 1861 and 1862, having been walked more than 550 miles from Nowra to Melbourne by his strapper Dave Power rather than shipped, a preparation Keith Dunstan held up as the toughest in Cup history.

Arthur Boyd was one of Australia's best-known twentieth-century painters, celebrated for expressionistic works dealing with the Australian bush, love and loss, including his acclaimed series documenting the mistreatment of Aboriginal Australians.
